papers.version_note: arXiv 2309.11617v2, 16 Apr 2024; the text layer ends with a note referring to Wiley Online Library supporting information. The record id says 2024 and the file name says 2023.
papers.what_it_is: A review and extension of the information-theoretic complexity of quantum learning that introduces copy complexity, with generalization and knowledge-gap bounds for supervised quantum state classification and a survey of generative models.

existing.value: The authors state they introduce copy complexity, the number of copies of a quantum state required to achieve a target accuracy, which arises from the destructive nature of quantum measurements.
quotes: Second, it introduces the notion of copy complexity, which quantiﬁes the number of copies of a quantum state required to achieve a target accuracy level.
Copy complexity arises from the destructive nature of quantum measurements
existing.certainty_reason: The abstract and Section 1.1 define the term.

existing.value: The authors state that in a quantum system it is generally not possible to evaluate the training loss on several hypotheses with the same quantum data, making empirical risk minimization generally inapplicable.
quotes: it is generally not possible to evaluate the training loss simultaneously on multiple hypotheses using the same quantum data, making empirical risk minimization generally inapplicable
existing.certainty_reason: The abstract states the scope of the setting; Section 1.1 repeats it.

existing.note: The paper omits a discussion of quantum advantage for the two reasons stated, but the same paragraph then names future directions toward advantage and conjectures a link between advantage in compressing classical data and advantage in learning. The first reason is caveats of real-world advantage claims, with ad-hoc data sets as the supporting point.
existing.value: The authors state they deliberately omit any discussion of quantum advantage for machine learning, giving two reasons: advantage in learning with real-world problems has several caveats, and it is complicated to define the best classical approach for a fair comparison. They add that most advantage results involve ad-hoc data sets built to beat the best classical approach, and then mention future directions on advantage.
quotes: we have deliberately omitted any discussion about quantum advantage for machine learning for two reasons
Most results about quantum advantage for machine learning involve ad-hoc datasets
Secondly, it is often complicated to deﬁne what the best classical approach is so as to make a fair comparison between quantum and classical learning.
Nonetheless, we mention here some future directions to explore the possibility of quantum advantage within the framework presented in this paper.
existing.certainty_reason: Section 7 states what the paper leaves out and why.

existing.note: Section 1.5.1 states the same gradient-evaluation mechanism as setup; the efficiency claim is the authors' own, untested.
existing.value: The authors state that each gradient evaluation of a quantum neural network consumes copies of the training data, so it is unlikely that quantum neural networks with many parameters use their copies efficiently.
quotes: each gradient evaluation requires the consumption of copies of the training data, so it is unlikely that quantum neural networks with many parameters make an eﬃcient use of their copies
existing.certainty_reason: The authors' own claim, not tested in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors define S as the number of copies of each training example and V as the number of copies of a test state, and call the requirements on V to achieve target accuracy the testing copy complexity.
quotes: We will use the letter S to indicate the number of copies of each training data example.
We will use the letter V to denote the number of copies of a test state, and refer to the requirements on V to achieve target accuracy levels as the testing copy complexity.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 1.1 states the definitions.

assertions.value: The authors state that classical data, barring computational complexity constraints, can be accessed, copied and processed an arbitrary number of times, and that the information extractable from quantum data depends on the number of copies available per state.
quotes: the amount of information that can be extracted from quantum data depends on the number of copies available for each quantum state in the data set
This stands in contrast to classical data, which, barring computational complexity constraints, can be accessed, copied, and processed an arbitrary number of times.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 1.1 states the premise of the setting.

assertions.value: The authors distinguish known training states, unknown training states with a known preparation mechanism, and unknown states with an unknown preparation mechanism, the last reduced to the second by setting S = 1.
quotes: Known training quantum states:
Unknown training quantum states, known state-preparation mechanism:
This extreme case may be reduced to the previous one by setting S = 1, i.e., each training state is treated as an individual copy.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 1.3 defines the settings.

assertions.value: The authors define inductive learning as extracting a classically describable rule from training data that is applied to any number of test examples, and transductive learning as jointly processing an S-copy training set with the test example, which requires distinct copies of the training data for each test example.
quotes: Importantly, the rule f can be applied to any number of test examples, and training examples are no longer needed after the training phase.
producing the output y for diﬀerent test examples (x, ρ(x)⊗V ) generally requires distinct copies of the training data.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 1.4 defines both terms.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing reference 18, that there are transductive strategies for predicting properties of physical systems, quantum principal component analysis and learning dynamics of n-qubit states that need exponentially fewer samples in n than inductive strategies that measure each state separately.
quotes: it has been shown[18] that there are transductive strategies for predicting properties of physical systems, performing quantum principal component analysis,
learning about the physical dynamics of n-qubit states that require exponentially fewer (in n) samples than inductive strategies that measure each state separately
assertions.certainty_reason: A result attributed to reference 18.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum neural networks are typically trained by gradient descent whose gradient is evaluated by measurements, requiring copies of the training data for each gradient evaluation.
quotes: whereby the gradient is evaluated by taking measurements of the output of the circuit, and variations thereof, thus requiring copies of the training data for each gradient evaluation
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 1.5.1 describes the training procedure it analyzes.

assertions.value: The authors decompose the test loss with an S-copy training set into terms including the excess testing error and the knowledge gap, and state that the analysis of these terms is the main new contribution of the work.
quotes: we refer to this diﬀerence as the excess testing error
The knowledge gap is always positive and depends on the learning strategy.
The analysis of these terms constitutes the main new contribution of this work.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 1.6.2 defines the quantities and states the claim.

assertions.value: The authors state that the optimal measurement for binary classification, which attains the minimum average loss, is the Holevo-Helstrom measurement, which involves the eigendecomposition of the difference of the class-average states.
quotes: The optimal measurement for binary classiﬁcation, which attains the minimum average loss LP , is known as the Holevo-Helstrom (HH) measurement
assertions.certainty_reason: A classical result of Helstrom and Holevo stated as background.

assertions.value: The authors state that their approximate bound 14, proved by Rademacher complexity analysis of unconstrained measurements or observables, shows generalization with few training examples is possible when the input space is small or the quantum states do not depend much on the input.
quotes: The above result is proved by analyzing the so-called Rademacher complexity of classes involving unconstrained generalized measurements or unconstrained observables.

The approximate inequality (14) shows that generalization with few training examples N is possible when either the input space is small or the quantum states ρ(x) do not depend too much on the input x.
assertions.certainty_reason: The bound itself is garbled in the text layer, so the statement and its conditions could not be quoted; Appendix B part 2 holds the proof.
assertions.reader_inference: The bound is an upper bound; the quoted sentence is the authors' reading of it.

assertions.value: The authors state that tomography-based approaches are not practical for large dimensional systems because the Hilbert space dimension grows exponentially with the number of qubits.
quotes: Accordingly, tomographic approaches are not practical for large dimensional systems, since the dimension of the Hilbert space d grows exponentially with the number of qubits.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 1.7 states the limit.

assertions.value: The authors state that the transductive strategy using phase estimation and state exponentiation has a knowledge gap with no dependence on the Hilbert space dimension, and that its scaling in N S is worse than for the tomography-based inductive approach.
quotes: Ignoring logarithmic corrections, the knowledge gap scales as ESS = O((N S)−1/3), without any dependence on the dimension d
That said, the scaling of the knowledge gap with N S is worse than for the tomography-based inductive approach.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated in the overview; the derivation is in Sections 4.5 and 5.2 (a sketch with stated assumptions).

assertions.value: The authors state that if N goes to infinity with S fixed, both the generalization error and the knowledge gap tend to zero.
quotes: if we let N → ∞ and keep S ﬁxed, both the generalization error and the knowledge gap tend to zero
assertions.certainty_reason: Argued in prose from the learner seeing infinitely many copies of every state with nonzero probability.

assertions.value: The authors state that, by the data processing inequality, constraining the output space reduces the mutual information that dictates the minimum average loss and the one that bounds generalization error, so the minimum average loss generally increases while the generalization error is expected to decrease.
quotes: By the data processing inequality, this operation reduces both the mutual information between quantum state and output label, which dictates the minimum average loss (11),

Therefore, constraining the output space generally causes the minimum average loss to increase, since some important information about the output label may be lost, while the generalization error is expected to decrease.
assertions.certainty_reason: Follows from the data processing inequality applied to the bounds; stated in prose, not as a numbered theorem.

assertions.value: The authors state that uniform-deviation bounds measure the worst-case generalization error over the whole function class and may predict overfitting even when the model generalizes well in practice.
quotes: Consequently, uniformdeviation bounds may predict overﬁtting, and hence poor generalization, even when the model generalize well in practice.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 1.8 states this limit of the method.

assertions.value: The authors state that if the states can be classified using local observables, about O(2 to the k) samples (printed flat as 2k) suffice for low generalization error when the label information is preserved by the locality projection.
quotes: In other words, if the states can be classiﬁed using local observables, at most N ≈ O(2k) samples are required to
assertions.certainty_reason: Derived from the mutual information bound with an approximate sign; the conditions on the label information are partly garbled.

assertions.value: The authors state that recent works characterized the generalization error of quantum neural networks and that reference 13 bounds it in terms of the number of trainable gates Ng.
quotes: Recent works [12, 13, 43] have characterized the generalization error of QNNs.
where Ng is the number of trainable gates in the QNN.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result attributed to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that their bound shows a large number of Fourier frequencies in the model requires more data to ensure generalization, and that their result applies to classification rather than only regression.
quotes: Our bound shows that a large number of Fourier frequencies in the model entails that more data are required to ensure generalization.
Our result (23) diﬀers from the ones in the literature, as it can be applied to classiﬁcation, rather than regression problems.
assertions.certainty_reason: Derived in Appendix C; the bound formula itself is garbled in the text layer.

assertions.value: The authors state that when the order parameter is a combination of k-local observables, the classification of phases can be learned with a number of data scaling at most as 2 to the k, and that whether the bounds explain generalization for global or topological order parameters is an open question.
quotes: we expect that this model can be learnt eﬃciently, using a number of data which scales at most as 2k.
generalization is less trivial, and whether the information theoretic bounds can provide an explanation is an open question
assertions.certainty_reason: An expectation from the bounds, supported by a numerical Ising experiment in reference 8.

assertions.value: The authors state that, by their bound, the number of samples to learn to classify separable against maximally entangled states grows exponentially with the number of qubits without prior structure, but that mapping the two-copy states by local twirling to a single-qubit state makes the mutual information constant so few training data are required.
quotes: the number of samples to learn to classify entanglement grows exponentially with n.
the mutual information is a constant, I1/2(X:QN ) = O(1), and we recover the expected result that few training data are required to learn this process.
assertions.certainty_reason: Derived from an upper bound in a toy problem; no experiment.
assertions.reader_inference: The exponential growth is a property of the upper bound, not shown as a lower bound on the sample need.

assertions.value: The authors state that the capacity-based analysis leaves out the impact of the training algorithm and of the data distribution, and that for deep networks the Rademacher bounds become vacuous.
quotes: This discussion points to some of the limitations of the capacity-based analysis presented in this work.
making the bounds (39) vacuous
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 2.2 states the limits.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing the no-cloning theorem, that copies of an unknown state cannot be produced, but different copies can be made if the recipe to build the state is known.
quotes: due to the no-cloning theorem [73], one cannot produce copies of an unknown state
diﬀerent copies of the state can be made if the recipe to build such state is known
assertions.certainty_reason: A standard physical result cited from reference 73.

assertions.value: The authors state that the optimal Helstrom measurement on multiple copies is in general highly non-local and requires coherent measurement over all copies, while simpler adaptive strategies are only known to be optimal for some classes such as pure states.
quotes: However, the resulting optimal Helstrom measurement in (58) is in general highly non-local, requiring the application of coherent measurements over all V copies of the state.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3.3 states the limit.

assertions.value: The authors state that, even without the optimal global measurements, if a local measurement distinguishes the states with probability above 1/2, perfect discrimination is obtained in the limit of many shots V by majority vote.
quotes: We conclude that, even without the optimal global measurements (58), provided that the local measurement is able to distinguish the state with probability (61) above chance, i.e., larger than 1/2, perfect discrimination can be obtained in the limit of many measurement shots V
assertions.certainty_reason: Argued with a large-V approximation of the binomial tail rather than a numbered theorem.

assertions.value: The authors state that the probability of error with an optimal measurement decreases exponentially with the number of copies as long as the two states are not identical, and that the majority-rule exponent is generally suboptimal.
quotes: Therefore, the probability of error with an optimal measurement decreases exponentially with the number of copies, as long as the two states are not identical,
Note that, as compared to the probability (59) for optimal global measurements, the exponent of the probability of error is generally suboptimal.
assertions.certainty_reason: Follows from the Fuchs-van de Graaf inequalities cited in the text.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer prints the fidelity condition as an equality to 1; the sense is that the fidelity is not 1.

assertions.value: The authors state that when the single-shot standard deviation is not small relative to the expectation value, the observable-based classifier uses an unreliable approximation and is known to be vulnerable to adversarial attacks, citing references 76 and 77.
quotes: When this is not the case, the model (62) uses an unreliable approximation of the actual empirical average to produce a decision.
Furthermore, in this regime, the classiﬁer is known to be vulnerable to adversarial attacks [76, 77], since tiny perturbations in the inputs can alter the prediction of the classiﬁer.
assertions.certainty_reason: The adversarial vulnerability is attributed to references 76 and 77.

assertions.value: The authors state that with the squared Hilbert-Schmidt norm as penalty, the representer theorem gives the optimal observable as a linear combination of the two possible states.
quotes: by the representer theorem, the optimal solution of problem (69) can be always expressed as a linear combination of the two possible states
assertions.certainty_reason: A classical result applied here, attributed to references 7 and 38.

assertions.value: The authors state that in the special case of pure states the optimal predictor computes the fidelities of the test state with the two states and outputs the class with the larger overlap, and that more shots are needed when the overlap between the two states is larger.
quotes: the optimal predictor (62) computes the ﬁdelities, or overlaps, Tr[ρρ+] and Tr[ρρ−], and outputs y = +1 or y = −1 depending on whether the ﬁrst or the second is larger than the other.
Accordingly, for larger overlaps F between the two possible states, one needs more shots V to resolve the diﬀerences between the two states with suﬃciently high probability.
assertions.certainty_reason: Derived for pure states under a hinge loss with the Hilbert-Schmidt penalty.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing reference 81, that full state tomography requires S = O(d2/ǫ2) copies of a d-dimensional state for precision ǫ in trace distance (exponents printed flat in the text layer; read as d squared over epsilon squared).
quotes: It is known that [81] full state tomography requires S = O(d2/ǫ2) copies of a d-dimensional state to obtain an approximate classical description with precision ǫ in the trace distance.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result attributed to reference 81.
assertions.reader_inference: Section 4.5 later writes the same cost as O(d2/ǫ), with epsilon to the first power; the two statements differ.

assertions.value: The authors state that if ηemp < 2ǫ the empirically constructed Helstrom measurement can be the worst rather than the best choice on the true states.
quotes: Conversely, if ηemp < 2ǫ, the empirically constructed measurement can be the worst, rather than the best, choice on the true states.
assertions.certainty_reason: Argued in the text with an example of states as linear combinations of the reconstructions.

assertions.value: The authors state that, although classical shadows can reconstruct exponentially many observables, it is unclear whether the advantage persists over families of observables, and so unclear whether shadow tomography gives an exponential advantage for state discrimination.
quotes: it is unclear whether the shadow tomography approach can provide an exponential advantage for state discrimination
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 4.2 states the open question.

assertions.value: The authors state that for a fixed measurement with K outcomes and the zero-one loss, the Rademacher complexity bound depends on the Renyi entropy of the measurement outcome distribution on the average state, that POVMs with fewer outcomes are preferable, and that a measurement with smaller entropy may have a larger training error.
quotes: Moreover, since 2H1/2(M) ≤ K, POVMs with fewer outcomes are preferable, in line with a similar bound that we get from support vector machines and neural networks (85).
so a measurement with a smaller value of H1/2(M) may have a larger training error
assertions.certainty_reason: The bound formula is garbled in the text layer; the proof rests on Theorem A.9 and Corollary A.10.

assertions.value: The authors state that when the observable is optimized over its spectral decomposition, the probability distribution of the outcomes also changes, so the setting is more similar to reinforcement learning than to supervised learning.
quotes: This setting is more similar to reinforcement, rather than supervised, learning.
assertions.certainty_reason: A remark without a derivation.

assertions.value: The authors state that the approximate Helstrom measurement via state exponentiation and phase estimation needs S = O(− log(ǫ)ǫ−3) copies of each state for failure probability at most ǫ (epsilon to the minus 3, printed flat), that the number of copies does not depend on the dimension, and that this requires manipulating all copies coherently.
quotes: Finally, we can say that we can enact the Helstrom measurement with a failure probability of at most ǫ using S = O(− log(ǫ)ǫ−3) copies of ρ+ and ρ−.
However, for the approximate Helstrom measurement scheme, the number of copies does not depend on the dimension of the states at all, so it can be more eﬃcient for high-dimensional states.
This eﬃciency comes at the price of having to manipulate all copies coherently.
assertions.certainty_reason: A derivation with a stated assumption that each unitary has the same error, not a formal theorem.
assertions.reader_inference: The text compares this with tomography cost O(d2/ǫ) here, which differs from the O(d2/ǫ2) of Section 4.2.

assertions.value: The authors state that exploiting the analytic solution of the representer-theorem strategy is expected to reach the same accuracy with fewer copies of the two states than the generic bound.
quotes: Therefore, exploiting the analytic solution (75) is expected to provide an advantage to get the same accuracy with fewer copies of the two states.
assertions.certainty_reason: Compares two upper bounds for pure states; the authors write expected.

assertions.value: The authors state that the scaling with the number of test copies V is worse for a transductive process than for an inductive one, by an amount that depends on how the single-copy error depends on S.
quotes: The scaling with V will therefore be worse than for an inductive process – how much worse depends on how the single-copy error depends on S.
assertions.certainty_reason: Argued by splitting the training set among V test states.

assertions.value: The authors state that if V is at most polynomial in n and ǫ is independent of n, the transductive strategy may provide an exponential advantage in n over tomography-based methods, while in the big data regime where V is large the inductive strategy may be preferable.
quotes: if V is at most polynomial in n and ǫ is independent on n, the transductive strategy may provide an exponential (in n) advantage compared with tomography based methods.
On the other hand, in the “big data” regime, where V is large, the inductive strategy may be preferable.
assertions.certainty_reason: Compares the two upper bounds of the displayed comparison; hedged with may.
assertions.reader_inference: The comparison is between upper bounds for specific protocols, not a proved separation.

assertions.value: The authors state that their Rademacher complexity bound proves the conjecture of reference 8 that the generalization error only slightly increases with the number of copies used in the majority vote, while the training error decreases exponentially in V.
assertions.anchor: Section 5.1.1, p.39; Appendix B part 3, p.53
quotes: thus providing a proof of the conjecture from [8], namely that the generalization error only slightly increases with the number of copies used in the majority vote.
Since the training error decreases exponentially with V , using more shots is expected to be beneﬁcial, as long as we have enough data to make (104) small.
assertions.certainty_reason: A proof is given in Appendix B part 3 but the bound formula is garbled in the text layer.

assertions.value: The authors state that with S going to infinity only the generalization error remains, with a single copy per state only the knowledge gap remains, and that for large finite S both appear.
quotes: so that the only source of error is the generalization error (with no excess testing error or knowledge gap)
We have no generalization error, since the average states ρ¯+ and ρ¯− are precisely what we want to discriminate between, and so the only source of error is the knowledge gap.
assertions.certainty_reason: Argued in prose for the two extremes.

assertions.value: The authors state that for tomography-based classification increasing S decreases only the knowledge gap, increasing N decreases both errors, and for large d the knowledge gap dominates.
quotes: Thus, increasing S decreases only the knowledge gap, whilst increasing N decreases both the knowledge gap and the generalization error. For large d, the knowledge gap will dominate.
assertions.certainty_reason: Follows from the tomography knowledge-gap scaling and the Rademacher bound.

assertions.value: The authors state that for the approximate Helstrom measurement via state exponentiation, if neither the knowledge gap nor the generalization error is to dominate for large N, S must also be increased.
quotes: Thus, if we do not want either the knowledge gap or the generalization error to dominate (for large enough N ), we must also increase S.
assertions.certainty_reason: Follows from combining the two error scalings of the section.

assertions.value: The authors state that for imperfect copies produced by a slow environment, if V is of order S the dependence on S and V disappears from the generalization error, at the price of a different mutual information that includes the environment.
quotes: Therefore, if V = O(S) the dependence on either S and V disappears from the generalization error, making it independent on the number of copies employed either during training or testing.
However, the price to pay is modeled by a diﬀerent mutual information
assertions.certainty_reason: Follows from the displayed bound, whose formula is garbled in the text layer.

assertions.value: The authors state that for observables with bounded 2-norm the generalization bound does not explicitly depend on properties of the quantum state, and that for Pauli-sum observables the bound grows exponentially with the number of qubits unless the coefficients are rescaled by an exponentially small quantity.
quotes: For observables with bounded 2-norm, generalization does not explicitly depend on the properties of the quantum state.
Therefore, unless the coeﬃcients αj are rescaled with an exponentially small quantity, the bound (113) grows exponentially with the number of qubits.
assertions.certainty_reason: Derived in Appendix B part 4.

assertions.value: The authors state that for observables with maximum eigenvalue equal to 1 the generalization bound is equivalent to that for optimizing over POVMs, and for the hinge loss the bounds are exactly equal.
quotes: For observables with maximum eigenvalue equal to 1, we can focus on G∞ with c∞ = 1
For the hinge loss, where λ = 1, the bounds are exactly equal.
assertions.certainty_reason: Derived in Appendix B part 4.

assertions.value: The authors state that classifying a new state with the kernel expansion requires evaluating new kernels, which consumes further copies of the training states, so the strategy is transductive.
quotes: Notice that for prediction the evaluation of new kernels k(xn, x) is necessary, which requires further copies of the training states ρ(xn), as discussed in Section 1.
This strategy is therefore transductive.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 5.5 states the setup of the strategy.

assertions.value: The authors state that the error with S copies scales as O(S to the minus 1/2) with a prefactor that diverges when the two average states are close, so less distinguishable states need more shots.
quotes: In this way, we can use Eq. (95) to show that the error using S copies scales as O(S−1/2), but with a prefactor that diverges when ρS+ ≃ ρ¯S−.
Accordingly, if the states are less distinguishable more shots are required.
assertions.certainty_reason: A lower bound from Jensen's inequality, not a full analysis of the kernel loss.

assertions.value: The authors state that both the Caro et al and Du et al bounds show that PQCs with many trainable gates incur a larger generalization error on a fixed number of examples, and that the Du et al bound suggests gate noise may not hurt generalization.
quotes: both bounds show that PQCs with large number of trainable gates, Ng, incur a larger generalization error when trained on a ﬁxed set of N examples
may not be detrimental to generalization and can help prevent over-ﬁtting
assertions.certainty_reason: Results attributed to references 13, 43 and 89.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Rademacher bounds of Caro et al and Du et al, which scale with the number of trainable parameters, cannot explain the low generalization error of QNNs observed in the over-parameterized regime, and that an encoding-based bound can help.
quotes: cannot explain the low generalization error of QNNs observed in the over-parameterized [90] regime
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 5.6 states the limit of the cited bounds.

assertions.value: The authors state that characterizing the excess risk of quantum generative models that approximate an unknown quantum state from S copies is an open problem, and that generalization analysis of quantum generative models has been studied in very few works.
quotes: Characterizing the excess risk in this setting is an open problem.
the generalization analysis of quantum generative models has been studied in very few existing works
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 6.3 states the open problem.

assertions.value: The authors state that the total error at test time may be decomposed as a sum of three terms: the error with known data distribution and states, the extra generalization error, and the extra knowledge gap, and that which method best exploits the training information is an open question.
quotes: The total error at the test stage, when the learnt model is used to make new predictions, may be decomposed as a sum of these three terms.
it is an open question to understand which method is
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 7 states the decomposition and the open question.

assertions.value: The authors state that identifying the most efficient strategy that minimizes all three sources of error with the least training resources is still an open question, and that the Helstrom classifier uses unconstrained operations so is unlikely to be optimal for generalization.
quotes: is still an open question
However, since the Helstrom classiﬁer uses unconstrained operations, it is unlikely to be optimal for generalization.
assertions.certainty_reason: The first is a stated open question; the second is an unproved expectation.

assertions.value: The authors state that, since quantum states can be used to compress classical data without losing predictive power, it is tempting to conjecture a link between quantum advantage in compressing classical data and quantum advantage in learning.
quotes: it is tempting to conjecture a link between quantum advantage in compressing classical data and quantum advantage in learning, namely in achieving the same accuracy with less data
assertions.certainty_reason: A conjecture without evidence in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that they use a worst-case formulation, maximizing the minimum detection probability over all pairs of states, and that the optimal Bayesian measurement may not be expressible as an inductive strategy.
quotes: This is the formulation we use in this article.
There is no guarantee that the optimal measurement from Eq. (D2) can be expressed in this form.
assertions.certainty_reason: Appendix D states the formulation the paper uses.

assertions.value: The paper restates, credited to Blanchard and reference 104, a bound on the empirical Rademacher complexity of the zero-one loss for functions constant on each cell of a partition of the input space, in terms of the cell counts Ni over N.
quotes: Theorem A.9 (credited to Blanchard[25, 104]).
The empirical Rademacher complexity of the 0-1 loss for function class F± and training set S satisﬁes
assertions.certainty_reason: Credited to other work; the bound formula is garbled in the text layer.

assertions.value: The paper presents Corollary A.11 as new: for real-valued functions constant on each cell of a partition with bounded norm and a Lipschitz margin loss, it bounds the empirical Rademacher complexity (one norm case by a constant over the square root of N, the other by a term in the cell counts).
quotes: We now present a new corollary.
Corollary A.11. Consider an input space X and a partitioning of X into K disjoint subsets Ki
The empirical Rademacher complexity of such a loss satisﬁes
assertions.certainty_reason: Proof given in the paper; the displayed bounds are partly garbled in the text layer.
